editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

div0.p: Tape AFC 2001/001/298 SR01 Interview with Frank Harper February 4, 2002 Transcribed and Processed by Maryann T. Murphy on 6/15/03 Frank N. Harper 2 February 4, 2002

sp.speaker: Emmy Huffman
sp.p: This interview is with Frank Harper.
He was born June 29th, 1923. Today is February 4th, 2002. We're doing the interview in his home in New Castle, Indiana. He served in the Army during World War II, and his highest rank was Sergeant.
When did you get drafted?

sp.speaker: Frank Harper
sp.p: It was in...well, I took my physical the last of February of '43, and I went in service full-time March the 6th, and I was inducted at Fort Benjamin Harrison.

sp.speaker: Emmy Huffman
sp.p: Where did you go to basic training?

sp.speaker: Frank Harper
sp.p: I took my basic training...at that time, it was Main Camp Hood Texas, and I was at Fort Hood and took my basic training there. Then from there, we were shipped to Arizona to Camp Laguna at the 743rd Tank Battalion.

sp.speaker: Emmy Huffman
sp.p: How long did you train in Arizona before you were sent to Europe?

sp.speaker: Frank Harper
sp.p: Well, let's see. We got out there...we were just replacements to the 743rd, what...
the group that I went with.

sp.speaker: Emmy Huffman
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Frank Harper
sp.p: And we left there in first of November of '43 for the...to go over in England and that.

We went to New Jersey and then went over to England. We landed in...lets's see. I was on the ship seven days, and that was the Aquitania. It was supposed to be the third largest luxury liner in the world at that time.

sp.speaker: Emmy Huffman
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Frank Harper
sp.p: And it was a British ship. We left Glasgow,
England, went on down to the Camp Chisbin (ph) which our first meal from the battalion kitchen was Thanksgiving.

sp.speaker: Emmy Huffman
sp.p: And were you in 1944 or '43?

sp.speaker: Frank Harper
sp.p: No. It was in '43 and that, which when I got in line and the turkey was already gone, I ate pork chops. It was just one of those things that happened and that. And then we trained, oh for, let's see, six months there in England where we landed in the D-Day.

sp.speaker: Emmy Huffman
sp.p: Did you know you were training for invasion of France?

sp.speaker: Frank Harper
sp.p: Yes. We had...we had special tanks. They were secret. There were Sherman tank, what they called the DB (ph) tank, which there is not many organizations that really had seen one or knew about them. And as of today there at Patton's museum at Fort Knox, there is none down there.

sp.speaker: Emmy Huffman
sp.p: Really?

sp.speaker: Frank Harper
sp.p: Because he had never...didn't have to use them. They were used for by the Seventh Tank Battalion, the 741st Tank Battalion, the 743rd Tank Battalion for D-Day. We all went in D-Day at Omaha Beach, which they floated in water.
The tank itself was submerged.

sp.speaker: Emmy Huffman
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Frank Harper
sp.p: But our colonel, he was Colonel John Uppen (ph). At that time, the D-Day, had the...maybe take us all of the way in because the Channel was so rough, a 30-caliber machine gun would sink them, and a big wave go over there would sink them. And which they were used, and there is a picture in this book of that. I don't think many people really realize what a BD (ph) tank was.

sp.speaker: Emmy Huffman
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Frank Harper
sp.p: Because everything was secret at that time on...even our training was secret over there for D-Day.

sp.speaker: Emmy Huffman
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Frank Harper
sp.p: And now does that look like a Sherman tank?

sp.speaker: Emmy Huffman
sp.p: I've never seen one before.

sp.speaker: Frank Harper
sp.p: No? And that...there may be... now, they got a new museum down in New Orleans, a D-Day museum down there. Have you ever heard of it?

sp.speaker: Emmy Huffman
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Frank Harper
sp.p: They could have one down there and that.

sp.speaker: Emmy Huffman
sp.p: So when you landed on Omaha Beach, did the tanks come after most of the troops had already landed or...

sp.speaker: Frank Harper
sp.p: Uh, well, we went in with the troops.

sp.speaker: Emmy Huffman
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Frank Harper
sp.p: What we could get in there, because the Channel was so rough and there were a thing... we were supposed to go in with the engineers...

sp.speaker: Emmy Huffman
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Frank Harper
sp.p: And that, but everything was grounded and that. People were everywhere and that, and a lot of our tanks never made it to the beach itself because of the water and everything, and a lot of them got sunk right before they hit the beach, and a few of them got hit and that, so...

sp.speaker: Emmy Huffman
sp.p: So your tank made it onto the beach then?

sp.speaker: Frank Harper
sp.p: I think...if I remember right, we got hit and then it disabled the tank, and then we scrambled up on foot, of which a lot of us went, got up on foot. And what tanks there were and what people that they needed help, we all went together and got what tanks we could up past the beach up the hill and that. And I got...what I got doing immediately was working on the gasoline engines that run the generator that kept the batteries up, because there was...there wasn't room for all of us to go in the good...the tanks were still in action, so we filled in what we could and that until we got tanks ready to go. Some just had tracks off of them and you had to repair them and everything, and the service company didn't go in as we went in. They come back and come in the next day, if I remember right for that.
But that...by that, then we got up in the hedgerows. And it was a lot of (?smacking people?), and most of them were French women sniping at us.

sp.speaker: Emmy Huffman
sp.p: Really.

sp.speaker: Frank Harper
sp.p: They were the women that married the German soldiers over there, and they were trying that way, and the hedgerows they were...maybe we'd take a hedgerow one day, and the next day we'd lose two. We would just battle them out in and out like that, so...

sp.speaker: Emmy Huffman
sp.p: How long did it take to get past the hedgerows then?

sp.speaker: Frank Harper
sp.p: Well, I'm trying to think. We was there a good month in the hedgerows, maybe longer, because it was slow. Those hedgerows were maybe an acre or two of ground, and then it took a while. You didn't dare stick up your big gun barrel through the hedgerow because they could have just threw a hand grenade up in there, and there you was out of action again. They were hard to get through because we...Some tanks, they welded what they called forks on them, dig a hole through the hedgerows and take them out.
Then they got...put dozer blades on a few of them so it was just like a Caterpillar, the blade was, and that got them going through there and that.

sp.speaker: Emmy Huffman
sp.p: So after you did that, did you then...were you part of moving towards Germany?

sp.speaker: Frank Harper
sp.p: Well, we headed for Paris. I mean, that's what we wanted to, but we never made it. We were routed up through Belgium and Holland, the three...the infantry which we were attached to, and the tank battalion went up there in Belgium and went in Holland and went in in Germany up that way. But the third army, that was Patton's army.

sp.speaker: Emmy Huffman
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Frank Harper
sp.p: He got over in France 30 days after we got the Germans moving back, and we took the (?glory?) and went in with Patton.

sp.speaker: Emmy Huffman
sp.p: Were you then in Europe when Germany surrendered?

sp.speaker: Frank Harper
sp.p: Oh, yeah.

sp.speaker: Emmy Huffman
sp.p: What was that like?

sp.speaker: Frank Harper
sp.p: Oh, I don't know. We was...we were clear up on the Elbe River at that time, and there was not too much celebration because we was way up in Germany and that. That's where we met the Russians, on the Elbe River and that.

sp.speaker: Emmy Huffman
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Frank Harper
sp.p: And that's where our last tank was hit, in Magdenburg, Germany, and our last people were killed and that. And civilians was firing at us that night. Diehards, you know. They were Germans and that. But they missed me. I followed the lieutenant into there and missed me, then the second shot got him and that. They just hit the going over me, and we backed up and that and stayed there until next day.

Because in the big town, fighting at night where you couldn't see and that, it was awful dangerous for a tank and that. But we went in the next day and went all through there and never fired a shot, but there was time to get in there was...they had a bridge cross the Elbe River, and they wanted to get ahold of it so they wouldn't have to build one, but...oh, then we pulled out of there that next day and that and went down and started...let's see, went over the town of Thale and that and started occupying there. But before that, it was common goal like we was up...just got in Germany too long before the Battle of the Bulge, and we went down there. I had a brand new tank when I went down there, took a beatin' and that. It tells in this book all the actions that we done and that and...but that new tank got...one day, it got hit point-blank and that. We didn't penetrate. And then later on after it got it all back together, we hit double mines, followed a German tank, went through down his tracks, but it didn't work, blew both tracks off of it and that. So it was a bad situation down there, but we made it. We spent Christmas down there. We had dinner, and we rigged up a Christmas tree and that, and we had lights on it because we run them off the batteries of the tank. He had a couple of bottles of Champagne that we had and that, but we done all right.

But we didn't hit snow...well, the reason I got hit point-blank, we didn't have our tanks whitewashed in that snow, and I never did see the German tank that hit me and that. The lieutenant there at the light tank company kept telling me, and I kept moving out the Samoan (ph), and then I got clipped and that, so...but nobody was hurt. The assistant driver was banged up a little bit and that, but...

sp.speaker: Unidentified Speaker
sp.p: UNIDENTIFIED SPEAKER: ______________+.

sp.speaker: Frank Harper
sp.p: Oh, that was way back...I don't remember. A couple times was out and that, but it was in and out of those tanks, I was, and that. The one crew...the crew before this last one I got, the...Lieutenant Cornell, he was new to the outfit, little Second Lieutenant, and it was up in Germany and kept telling him to keep the front of that tank to the enemy. But he pulled it on the side of it, and they blast his side of it. And we didn't have no armor on the side of our tanks. We didn't have that much on the front. But that's why we put sand bags on it.
See, there where the sand bags?

sp.speaker: Emmy Huffman
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Frank Harper
sp.p: Down there where I got hit point blank in the Bulge, I just got the sand bags on that new tank, and that's the reason they didn't penetrate because they were with me froze. They were just like more armored on the front.

sp.speaker: Emmy Huffman
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Frank Harper
sp.p: But that...and sand bags and everything on them were for bazookas where they wouldn't penetrate, but what we couldn't put them up on the turret. That's where the last gunner got killed and lieutenant, because they put about the size of a silver dollar hole. They went in there. But when they get inside, they start burning. You've seen a cutting torch throw flames and sparks?

sp.speaker: Emmy Huffman
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Frank Harper
sp.p: Well, them little sparks are little pieces of shrapnel, red hot, and which it took the side of the...it took the gunner's arm all the way off, which...

sp.speaker: Emmy Huffman
sp.p: In your tank?

sp.speaker: Frank Harper
sp.p: No, in the lieutenant's tank. Now, he was the last one that would have been the lieutenant died after he got to the hospital.
But otherwise, we were...and that. We had a lot of people killed and that.

sp.speaker: Emmy Huffman
sp.p: Can you tell me about your Presidential Unit Citation?

sp.speaker: Frank Harper
sp.p: Well, that was for D-Day.

sp.speaker: Emmy Huffman
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Frank Harper
sp.p: The whole 743rd outfit received one for what we had done D-Day, landed D-Day. We got that for the invasion of Omaha there at D-Day and that.

sp.speaker: Emmy Huffman
sp.p: And how about your Bronze Star? When did you get that?

sp.speaker: Frank Harper
sp.p: Well, that was just more or less the whole European operation that I'd done, that's what...and that, because I was too brave. And most of them...I'd say most of the people that got one of them medals, there was always a good buddy of his always wrote up and sent it in, which I...but after the end of the war, I found out the more medals you got, the more points you got out, and the quicker you got home.

sp.speaker: Emmy Huffman
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Frank Harper
sp.p: And that, because all you needed was 85 points to get home.

sp.speaker: Emmy Huffman
sp.p: Do you mind if I read your citation into the...

sp.speaker: Frank Harper
sp.p: Go ahead.

sp.speaker: Emmy Huffman
sp.p: Okay. It says, "Sergeant, then Corporal, and Sergeant Frank N. Harper, 743rd Tank Battalion,
United States Army, is awarded the Bronze Star for heroic achievement in service from 6 June 1944 to 15 February 1945 in France, Belgium,

Holland and Germany. Sergeant Harper has distinguished himself by outstanding performance of duty as a gunner and tank commander. His skill and cool judgment have contributed to the successful completion of many hazardous missions throughout the bitter fighting across the Continent. Sergeant Harper's courage and devotion to duty reflect great credit on himself and the Armed Forces."

sp.speaker: Frank Harper
sp.p: Well, that picture was taken when I got...received that. That's General Hobbs of the 30th Division, and that picture was also in the Indianapolis Times in July of '45. And I did have that clipping, but it's...I just threw it away here a while back because you couldn't read it. It was faded out. I probably could go to the library and get another one, but I don't know.

sp.speaker: Emmy Huffman
sp.p: Did you write home a lot while you were in Europe?

sp.speaker: Frank Harper
sp.p: Not too much.

sp.speaker: Emmy Huffman
sp.p: Were you married then or...

sp.speaker: Frank Harper
sp.p: No. I wasn't married to her, because we got married in '47, January of '47. We have been married 55 years now.

sp.speaker: Emmy Huffman
sp.p: Congratulations.

sp.speaker: Frank Harper
sp.p: And that. But this is a Cold War certificate we just got. This is a picture was taken after the war. That's what tanks we had left. Them are...the old Sherman tanks that they didn't want right away because they were sending a lot of the tanks over to the Pacific, which this one we turned in right away. I turned that one in because that was the late-model one, but it wasn't the latest. The Patton was the latest, which we never got and that. Patton had the 90 on it. Well, that had the 76, and these others had the 75 on them and that.

sp.speaker: Emmy Huffman
sp.p: Did you think you were going to have to go to the Pacific?

sp.speaker: Frank Harper
sp.p: No. I knew I wouldn't have to because I had enough points. I didn't have to.

sp.speaker: Emmy Huffman
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Frank Harper
sp.p: See, the time you had in service counted, the time you had overseas counted so many points and that. My crew...most of these fellows, while they took...they took Crandall there...he was my driver...right away. And then the other three left, but...John Roughstead, he lives up in Billings, Montana. I contact him every so often and that. But these other three, I think, are already...are dead now, because he died, oh, maybe 20 years ago,
Crandall did. But he didn't have to go overseas. In fact, they got discharged before I did.

sp.speaker: Emmy Huffman
sp.p: Really?

sp.speaker: Frank Harper
sp.p: Yeah. Because they were home to go over in the Pacific, but that didn't happen. And I was still over there and waiting on the stripe, spent, oh, time over in Marseille, France, because no pay and just breaking up the unit on kind of a dock ____ in New York at that time and that. But otherwise...

sp.speaker: Emmy Huffman
sp.p: Do you stay...

sp.speaker: Frank Harper
sp.p: After the war, I did go to Paris. There is a picture in Paris. These are some of them.

sp.speaker: Emmy Huffman
sp.p: Did you see a lot of Europe then while you were over there?

sp.speaker: Frank Harper
sp.p: Oh, not after the war. But as we tore it up and that because...seen a lot of England, a lot of over there, as much as I can or could, I should say, and that. These are just little snapshots I took. Them are all taken over in England.

sp.speaker: Emmy Huffman
sp.p: Do you stay in contact with any of the rest of your tank crew?

sp.speaker: Frank Harper
sp.p: Well, just Johnny. He lives up in Billings,
Montana, and that. But...

sp.speaker: Emmy Huffman
sp.p: Have you ever gone to any unit reunions or anything?

sp.speaker: Frank Harper
sp.p: They had a reunion every two years up in Minneapolis. Last August was the last one.

Nobody showed up. They are just...people are dead, you know, and they are getting old and that. These are pictures of...this is Dominick and that. This was the one that's...he's...he was up, lives up in Billings, Montana.
Roughstead.

sp.speaker: Emmy Huffman
sp.p: Do you guys talk very much about the war?

sp.speaker: Frank Harper
sp.p: No, no, not too much and that. This is Rosenberg. He was...he had a couple of years of medical, and they didn't...wouldn't put him in the Medics. These...this crew right here...we was way up in Germany when the lieutenant took over my crew, and I had to break in a new crew.

This...they didn't go through the hedgerows or back through Belgium and that, which Belgium and Holland were...it wasn't much fighting through there. It was a lot of partying. Now, these are Christmas cards the colonel had sent me. And my original one that I had, I sent my folks from over there that Christmas. My grandson has got about...because he had some deals going through high school and that, same way he's got my picture on that. These are what we had. Colonel got messed up every time when he sent me one, but I kept in contact with him.
He was...he stayed in service. In fact, the colonel...the original colonel that got hit D-Day, they shipped him home and he stayed in.
He became a general. And Duncan there, he became a full bird. He stayed in, but he served under the other colonel while he was in, stayed in and that. I think because...let's see here.
This is a card he sent at one time. This is from '95. He was 84 then and that. This sent me in '96 and that. Wait a minute. I think his wife, more or less.

sp.speaker: Emmy Huffman
sp.p: Have you ever watched any movies like Saving Private Ryan about D-Day?

sp.speaker: Frank Harper
sp.p: Well, yeah. I've seen them all.

sp.speaker: Emmy Huffman
sp.p: What do you think of them?

sp.speaker: Frank Harper
sp.p: Well, there are, I would say, a lot of true things in it, but a lot of them was money- making for the movies and that. Same way with D-Day. Because now if you watched the Battle of the Bulge, the show...

sp.speaker: Emmy Huffman
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Frank Harper
sp.p: The tanks the Americans had were M-24's.

They were light tanks. They were with the 75 on it. But the ones the Germans had were the Patton tanks that we never got and that. But it's all fiction, you know, even with the Patton, which...those are the...actually, that's...my son wrote this one. He had that listed down there, the five battles, major battles we were in and that.

sp.speaker: Emmy Huffman
sp.p: When you got home back to the States, how much time did you have left in the service?

sp.speaker: Frank Harper
sp.p: How much time did I have left? Pulled in there, let's see, New Jersey one night, ate a big dinner. Next day, we got on the train, went to Camp Attabury, and I was there two days, discharged at 10:00 on Armistice Day, and I come on home. I got about a dollar and a half traveling pay from there, and that's...that was about it, but...

sp.speaker: Emmy Huffman
sp.p: When you got home then, did you go to school or did you start working right away?

sp.speaker: Frank Harper
sp.p: Oh, I had a good job when I went to service.

I worked at Herff Jones and that, and I went back to work there. Oh, I took a few days, a few weeks off and that. But I worked there and retired from there. But when I left there, I went...I wasn't old enough, really, to retire.

I went and worked a few other places and that because...oh, I had 30 years in, and I'm getting small pension from them, but it don't amount to much and that. But mainly these books show everybody was in our outfits, the Medical Corps and that. This book's getting bad now.
Each company, the light tank. Here is the company I was in and that. Had all of them.
But, actually, this here book right here, it's on the market. It sells for $29. That's what... my son got him one and this while he was out there and that. But it's got a few pictures, tells...

sp.speaker: Emmy Huffman
sp.p: How do you think your service and your time in Europe changed your life?

sp.speaker: Frank Harper
sp.p: It didn't change my life. I just...it was just the time I was in. I don't know. I was working. But I don't think it changed it any because I was too young to really, really pay much attention to it because I graduated just about in '41 from Ben Davis, and just about all my whole classmates went to service, and I don't think out of there there was only a couple of fellows that got killed and that.
Because we had a 50th reunion, and most of them were there. And the one fellow was Goldberg.

He stayed down Florida there at Cape, the Cape and in the...oh, the astronaut deal. And then the other fellow was still in service. He was a colonel in the Air Force. There was still, you know, and that, which I'd seen them. These here are all...I got one gone here that...where we went and that.

sp.speaker: Emmy Huffman
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Frank Harper
sp.p: Where we were and this more...I don't think my son...see, this is D-Day. I don't think my son...there might be one gone. Now this is...we were down in the Bulge, and we went down there...maybe not, and that. These were towns that we were all in and that. We took a beatin'. The other time, we had 52 tanks. I think we lost, oh, I think it was...it says in here. I don't remember the number. We lost more than we was, you know, the same way...of course, didn't we all? And that. But we were good. We were considered one of the best tank battalions the Army ever had and that, which, as I tell my son...because he stayed in service. He went to service. He spent more time in Germany than I had in service. As I tell him, we went in, got the job done, and come home. We didn't play around. But we partied and that.

sp.speaker: Emmy Huffman
sp.p: All right. Well, that's all I have to ask you. Is there anything else you want to say?

sp.speaker: Frank Harper
sp.p: Well, no, not really, but you can see what I have got, kept and that. These were...we were the only...in our company from Indiana, the only three and that.

sp.speaker: Emmy Huffman
sp.p: Really?

sp.speaker: Frank Harper
sp.p: Let's see. He got shot after the war. We were in the town. That was in Thale. It was like a park like. We had a guard sit up there, you know, for guard. And some of them old guns they had, what we called a grease gun and that, went off and shot him. And I...after that, I lost contact. But Fields there, he was from Huntington, Indiana, and that, so...but there was a...one fellow that was in the B Company that was from Indianapolis named Hamilton. Lost contact to him and that. Of course now...this picture right here, now you see that? There was a brick wall there, okay? That guy spent...that was in Germany on Gogetz (ph) right there on the Elbe River, and we couldn't get the tank down there without tearing so Larry took the track and knocked the wall down, a big brick fence. He stood there and watched us to get down to the river because they thought there was a bridge down there, which there wasn't.

It was just a ferry and that. But you mangled these walls down, went down there, come back, and we stayed there and that and set up a guard that night, went inside there and cooked...which what we really got, I'm sure it was supply...we got...we got a fresh loaf of white bread every day per crew and that, and we took it in there and they were surprised that we had white bread and that, but they were friendly. They...we wasn't supposed to fraternize with Germans back them days and that, so...but we did and that. These pictures I took, I don't remember where they were. They were somewhere in Germany and that. This is taken in Magdenburg, Germany. A lot of booze and that, so...but oh, well. It's just one of those things that part of my life, but I don't regret it and that. I was young and that, and I didn't spend that much time in. I got in and got out. My main thought was getting out alive...after we knew how far we had to go, it...my thoughts every night, am I going to make it the next day and that. But oh, I did.

I'm still doing pretty good, I guess. But there's not many of us left. Let's see, I got just three Christmas cards from three people and that. The one lives up in Minnesota. And Kinner, he lives in Omaha, and Johnny lives up there in Billings. But they were all the guys I knew, went overseas with, came home with and that. Or started home with, because after they broke us up, we didn't...they split us up here and there, and we just couldn't stay together.
But this book here, kept in contact. A lot of them are dead and that, so.

sp.speaker: Emmy Huffman
sp.p: Okay.
